knowledge.title: Mobile money in Somalia and Somaliland: EVC Plus, Zaad, Sahal, e-Dahab, Premier Wallet (Lacagaha moobaylka)
knowledge.text:
Somalia is one of the world's most mobile-money-dependent economies. Central Bank and operator figures suggest roughly 70% or more of adults use mobile money, while only around 15% have a bank account. Most mobile money is denominated in US dollars, because the old Somali shilling notes are scarce and largely counterfeit; in Somaliland, wallets are used in both Somaliland shillings and dollars. Payments for almost everything—groceries, taxis, rent, school fees, khat, utilities, salaries and humanitarian cash aid—are made by phone, often through USSD menus and increasingly via smartphone apps and QR codes.

Main services:
- EVC Plus (Hormuud Telecom): the largest platform, dominant in Mogadishu and south-central Somalia; launched around 2011, licensed by the Central Bank in 2021, and GSMA-certified. Hormuud says over 4.5 million people use it; studies estimate it handles the large majority of Somali mobile money transactions. Hormuud also runs the Waafi app for international and wallet services and links EVC Plus with partner banks.
- Zaad (Telesom): the main service in Somaliland, launched in 2009, the first major Somali mobile money service; famous for free person-to-person transfers.
- Sahal (Golis Telecom): the main service in Puntland.
- e-Dahab (Somtel, linked to the Dahabshiil group): used across Somalia and Somaliland; Dahabshiil remittances can be received in e-Dahab.
- Premier Wallet (Premier Bank), eBesa (IBS Bank), MyCash and other bank wallets; services like Jeeb and T-Plus also exist.
Hormuud, Telesom and Golis are part of an affiliated group sometimes described as HTG, which historically limited interoperability between regions.

Infrastructure: the Central Bank launched the National Payment System in 2021 and in January 2025 introduced the Somalia Instant Payment System (SIPS) and the national QR standard SOMQR, aiming to make wallets and banks interoperable. Integration was still under way in 2026.

Common usage: users send money by dialling a USSD code and entering the recipient's number and amount; merchants display their merchant number; airtime and data bundles are bought with mobile money. Fees on person-to-person transfers are typically zero or very low; cash-out at agents may cost a small fee.

Safety guidance for an assistant: never ask for or store a user's PIN; warn about scams (fake "wrong transfer" calls, fake prize messages, impersonation of operator staff); suggest confirming the recipient name shown before approving; and advise contacting the operator's official customer service for disputes. Do not guess USSD codes—tell users to check their operator's official channels.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_money_in_Somalia; https://www.hormuud.com/Updates/Hormuud-Telecom-Receives-GSMA-Re-Certification-for-Secure-Mobile-Money-Services; https://academic.oup.com/ia/article/101/1/117/7942194; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-dynamics/articles/10.3389/fhumd.2025.1692506/full

knowledge.title: Telecoms and internet in Somalia (Isgaarsiinta iyo internetka)
knowledge.text:
Somalia's telecom sector developed privately during the years without a central state and is now one of the most competitive and affordable in Africa in cities, though rural coverage remains uneven.

Main operators (as of 2025–2026):
- Hormuud Telecom: the largest operator, headquartered in Mogadishu, dominant in south-central Somalia; provides mobile, 4G/5G, fibre home internet and EVC Plus.
- Somtel: national operator linked to the Dahabshiil group; mobile, internet and e-Dahab.
- Golis Telecom: main operator in Puntland (Sahal mobile money, FTTH internet, 5G packages).
- Telesom: main operator in Somaliland (Zaad mobile money).
- NationLink, Amtel, Somnet and other smaller operators and internet providers.
Hormuud, Golis and Telesom are affiliated companies (HTG group).

Regulation: the National Communications Authority (NCA, Hay'adda Isgaarsiinta Qaranka), set up under the 2017 Communications Act, licenses operators, manages numbering (country code +252) and spectrum. Somaliland and Puntland have their own regulators. Puntland and Somaliland users may have different numbering and operators from Mogadishu.

Internet: Somalia connects to the world through submarine cables (including EASSy, landed in Mogadishu in 2014, and DARE1, landed in 2021) and terrestrial links. 4G covers major cities and trade routes, and 5G has been rolled out in parts of major cities since the early 2020s. Home fibre (FTTH) is available in Mogadishu, Hargeysa, Garoowe and Boosaaso. Internet users were estimated at around 28–30% of the population in 2024, with about 11 million mobile connections in early 2025 (DataReportal). The NCA licensed Starlink satellite internet in April 2025 (10-year licence), and the service went live nationwide in August 2025, with kit prices starting around US$200–390 and monthly residential plans around US$70 at launch.

Outages: cable cuts have caused nationwide internet disruptions (e.g. in 2017 and 2024), and authorities have occasionally restricted social media or the internet during national exams or security events; in 2023 the government announced a ban on TikTok, Telegram and a betting site that was not consistently enforced.

Assistant guidance: when users report connectivity problems, suggest operator support and alternatives (Wi-Fi, other SIM); keep voice responses short where data is expensive or slow; do not assume users have unlimited data.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications_in_Somalia; https://nca.gov.so/national-communications-authority-grants-starlink-official-license-to-operate-in-somalia; https://www.telecompaper.com/news/starlink-launches-services-in-somalia--1544367; https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2025-somalia

knowledge.title: Currency: Somali shilling, US dollar and Somaliland shilling (Lacagta: shilin Soomaali, doollar, shilin Somaliland)
knowledge.text:
Somali shilling (SOS, shilin Soomaali): the official currency of Somalia, issued by the Central Bank of Somalia (Bankiga Dhexe ee Soomaaliya). One shilling is divided into 100 senti, but coins are not used. No new legitimate banknotes have been printed since 1990–1991; the notes in circulation, mainly the 1,000-shilling note, are old, worn and largely counterfeit copies printed by warlords and businessmen during the civil war. Physical shillings are used only for small purchases (e.g. vegetables, tea, transport fares); most transactions are in US dollars, in cash or mobile money. The Central Bank's 2025 annual report put the average market rate at roughly SOS 30,000 per US dollar in 2025 (rates fluctuate; check current figures).

New currency plan: the Central Bank is preparing to reintroduce a new series of Somali shilling banknotes with modern security features, backed by a Currency Board Arrangement anchored to the US dollar and supported by the IMF and the World Bank's Somalia Currency Exchange Project. As of October 2026, preparations were "at an advanced stage", parliament was considering amendments to the Central Bank Act, designs were being kept secret to deter counterfeiting, and no launch date had been announced. The IMF urged careful sequencing. A dual system with the shilling and the dollar circulating together is expected.

US dollar: prices for rent, goods, salaries, school fees, airline tickets and most mobile money transfers are quoted in dollars. Small dollar bills that are old or torn may be refused.

Somaliland shilling (SLSH): issued by the Bank of Somaliland since 1994, used in Somaliland alongside the dollar; it is not recognised outside Somaliland. Large stacks of notes are common for cash purchases, but Zaad mobile money dominates. Its exchange rate fluctuates and is quoted daily by money changers.

Other: in Puntland and the south, the old SOS notes circulate; Puntland has at times seen separate printings. Ethiopian birr is used in border areas and the Somali Region of Ethiopia; Kenyan shillings near the Kenyan border; Djiboutian francs in Djibouti.

Banking: Somalia has a growing Islamic banking sector (e.g. Premier Bank, Salaam Somali Bank, IBS Bank, Dahabshil Bank, Amal Bank, Amana Bank, MyBank, Agro Bank) licensed by the Central Bank, with IBAN numbers introduced for cross-border transfers. Interest-based (riba) products are generally avoided in favour of Islamic contracts like murabaha.

Assistant guidance: quote prices in USD unless the user uses shillings; give exchange rates only from current sources with dates.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_shilling; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somaliland_shilling; https://centralbank.gov.so/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Annual-Report_2025.pdf; https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/business-tech/somalia-moves-closer-to-restoring-own-currency-after-35-years-5570236

knowledge.title: Education and universities in Somalia (Waxbarashada iyo jaamacadaha)
knowledge.text:
Education in Somalia combines Qur'anic schooling, a formal school system run largely by private and community providers, and a large private university sector.

Qur'anic school (dugsi Quraan / malcaamad): most children start here around age 4–6, learning to read and memorise the Qur'an and basic Arabic. Many attend dugsi alongside formal school.

Formal school: the federal system is broadly structured as primary (8 years) and secondary (4 years), with national examinations administered by the federal Ministry of Education, Culture and Higher Education; Somaliland and Puntland run their own curricula and exams. Somali is the main language of instruction in early grades, with English and Arabic used increasingly in upper grades and at university. A large share of schools are private or run by umbrella networks (such as FPENS and SAPES) and charge fees; public schooling is expanding but limited. Millions of children, especially girls, nomadic and displaced children, are out of school. Adult literacy is low compared with regional averages.

History: Somali was first written officially in the Latin script in 1972, followed by mass literacy campaigns in 1973–1975. The Somali National University (Jaamacadda Ummadda Soomaaliyeed) grew from an institute founded in the 1950s and became a full university around 1970; it closed during the civil war and reopened in 2014.

Major universities (selection):
- Mogadishu: Somali National University (SNU), Mogadishu University (1997), SIMAD University (1999), Benadir University (2002, known for medicine), Jamhuriya University of Science and Technology, City University of Mogadishu, Plasma University, Zamzam University.
- Somaliland: University of Hargeisa (2000), Amoud University (Boorama, 1998), Gollis University (Hargeysa), Burao University.
- Puntland: Puntland State University (Garoowe), East Africa University (Boosaaso, with branches).
- Elsewhere: Kismayo University, University of Southern Somalia (Baydhabo), Galkayo University, Hiiraan University.
Accreditation and quality vary; the Commission for Higher Education regulates the federal sector. Many Somali students also study in Turkey, Sudan, Egypt, Malaysia, India, Kenya, Uganda and the Gulf, often on scholarships (e.g. Türkiye Scholarships).

Assistant guidance: when users ask about admissions, fees or exam results, direct them to official ministry or university websites and give dates as "as of"; help students with Somali/English study support without completing graded work dishonestly.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_National_University; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_in_Somalia; https://moe.gov.so/

knowledge.title: Health system basics in Somalia (Nidaamka caafimaadka)
knowledge.text:
Somalia's health system is fragile and largely privatised after decades of conflict. Public facilities exist but are underfunded; many services are delivered by private hospitals and clinics, NGOs and UN agencies, and diaspora-funded facilities.

Key health indicators (approximate, from UN/WHO estimates): life expectancy in the mid-to-high 50s; high maternal mortality and child mortality compared with world averages; low vaccination coverage in many areas; recurrent outbreaks of cholera/acute watery diarrhoea, measles and malnutrition, especially during droughts and floods. Mental health services are very limited, though awareness is growing.

Main hospitals (selection): in Mogadishu, the Somali Turkish Training and Research Hospital (often called "Erdoğan Hospital", opened 2015), Banadir Hospital (maternal and child), De Martino Hospital, Madina Hospital, Kalkaal and many private hospitals; in Hargeysa, Hargeisa Group Hospital and the Edna Adan Hospital (maternity and teaching hospital founded by Edna Adan Ismail, opened 2002); Garowe General Hospital and Bosaso General Hospital in Puntland; Kismayo General Hospital; Baidoa Regional Hospital.

Emergency: in Mogadishu, the free AAMIN Ambulance service (founded 2006) can be reached on 999, and is known for responding to bomb attacks and emergencies. Elsewhere, ambulance services are limited, and families often transport patients themselves.

Pharmacies (farmashiye) are widespread and often sell medicines, including antibiotics, without prescription; counterfeit or poor-quality drugs are a concern. Many people combine modern medicine with traditional remedies (e.g. black seed/habbatu sawdaa, honey, cauterisation "gubid", herbal medicine) and Qur'anic healing (ruqyah, "tafsiir/ruqyo").

Medical travel: those who can afford it travel abroad for treatment, especially to India, Turkey, Kenya (Nairobi), Ethiopia (Addis Ababa), Egypt and the UAE, often funded by relatives.

Health topics sensitive in Somali culture: mental illness (sometimes attributed to jinn), FGM, family planning and reproductive health; speak respectfully and practically.

Assistant guidance: the assistant is not a doctor. For symptoms, give general safe information, encourage seeing a qualified health worker, and for emergencies tell users to get urgent care (in Mogadishu, AAMIN 999). Never recommend stopping prescribed medication or replacing treatment with unproven remedies.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_in_Somalia; https://www.who.int/countries/som; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edna_Adan_University_Hospital; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aamin_Ambulance

knowledge.title: Government services, national ID and passports (Adeegyada dowladda, aqoonsiga qaranka iyo baasaboorka)
knowledge.text:
National ID (Aqoonsiga Qaranka) – Federal Government: the National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA; Hay'adda Diiwaangelinta iyo Aqoonsiga Qaranka) launched Somalia's first national ID system in September 2023 with World Bank support. As of September 2026, NIRA reported over 1.5 million citizens registered, 59 registration centres, 17 mobile teams, and 31 registration points at Somali embassies abroad, with a target of 15 million people by 2029. The ID is available as a physical card, a printable certificate with QR code, and in the eAqoonsi mobile app (launched August 2026). The Hubiye platform lets banks, telecoms and agencies verify identity. Registration is free. Card issuance has been limited or pending in Puntland, Jubaland and Somaliland for political or administrative reasons (as of 2026).

ID requirements: a NIRA ID or proof of NIRA registration is required to apply for a Somali passport (phased in from 2025–2026), and from 1 October 2026 the Immigration and Citizenship Agency began requiring national ID for domestic travel between regions, which disrupted some flights, notably to and from Puntland.

Passports: Somali passports are issued by the Immigration and Citizenship Agency (ICA; Hay'adda Socdaalka iyo Jinsiyadda, often abbreviated HSJ), with an online application portal (immigration.gov.so) and offices in Mogadishu, regional cities and some embassies. The current passport is biometric. The Somali passport offers visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to relatively few countries. Foreign visitors to Somalia apply for an electronic visa/travel authorisation online (a system that suffered a data breach in November 2025).

Somaliland issues its own ID cards and passports, recognised only by a few countries; many Somalilanders also hold Somali or foreign passports. Puntland has its own ID and registration systems.

Other services: business registration (Ministry of Commerce and Industry), tax (Ministry of Finance, Banadir Regional Administration for Mogadishu local taxes), land and property registration (often disputed), driving licences and vehicle plates (regional authorities), birth registration (low coverage, being expanded with NIRA), and courts. Many services are increasingly online or paid by mobile money.

Assistant guidance: rules change frequently; always tell users to confirm requirements and fees on official sites (nira.gov.so, immigration.gov.so) or offices, and give "as of" dates. Never ask for a user's full ID number unless needed for a specific task they request.
Sources: https://sonna.so/en/article/NIRA-Marks-World-ID-Day-Highlights-Progress-in-National-Registration; https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/nasikiliza/federal-republic-of-somalia-launches-mass-registration-drive-for-its-digital-id; https://somaliatoday.com/society/somalia-begins-enforcing-national-id-for-domestic-travel-2026-10-02/; https://www.ftlsomalia.com/nira-launches-eaqoonsi-digital-id-app-for-somali-citizens

knowledge.title: Popular apps and digital life among Somalis (Barnaamijyada iyo nolosha dhijitaalka)
knowledge.text:
Digital life among Somalis is mobile-first: most people go online through smartphones and affordable data bundles, and many older or rural users rely on basic phones with USSD menus and voice calls.

Most used platforms (based on usage reports and common observation, as of 2025–2026):
- WhatsApp: the main messaging tool for families, businesses, news groups, diaspora fundraising and voice notes. Voice notes are extremely popular, since many people prefer speaking Somali to typing it.
- Facebook: widely used for news, community pages, announcements (including death notices and job adverts) and business pages.
- TikTok: hugely popular among young Somalis for music, comedy, poetry, live streams and debates, and also a source of controversy over clan-based insults and misinformation. The government announced a ban in 2023 that was not consistently enforced, and in 2025 people were arrested over a satirical TikTok video about the president.
- YouTube: Somali music, films (Somali film and drama series), religious lectures, news channels and tutorials.
- Telegram, Instagram, Snapchat and X (Twitter): used by younger and diaspora users and by politicians and media.
- Mobile money and fintech apps: EVC Plus and the Waafi app (Hormuud), Zaad (Telesom), Sahal (Golis), e-Dahab and Somtel superapp, Premier Wallet, and bank apps.
- Government digital services: the eAqoonsi digital ID app (NIRA), online passport applications, eVisa.
- E-commerce and delivery services are growing in Mogadishu and Hargeysa, as are ride-hailing and taxi booking apps, mostly paid by mobile money.

Language online: Somalis write Somali in the Latin alphabet, often informally (skipping double vowels, mixing English, using numbers and abbreviations like "mhd" for mahadsanid). Arabic script is used for religious content. Many diaspora users mix Somali with English, Swedish, Norwegian, Dutch, etc.

Digital concerns: scams (fake mobile money messages, fake job offers), misinformation and hate speech during political tensions, online harassment of women, and privacy. Internet disruptions happen during cable cuts or exam periods.

Assistant guidance: expect informal spelling and voice input; reply in clear standard Somali (or the user's language), keep messages short for mobile screens, offer voice-friendly answers, and warn users about common scams when relevant.
Sources: https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2025-somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_Somalia; https://www.ftlsomalia.com/nira-launches-eaqoonsi-digital-id-app-for-somali-citizens; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications_in_Somalia

knowledge.title: Sport in Somalia: football, the Ocean Stars and athletics (Ciyaaraha: kubadda cagta, Ocean Stars)
knowledge.text:
Football (kubadda cagta) is by far the most popular sport among Somalis. People follow the English Premier League, Spanish La Liga and other European leagues intensely, watching in cafés and video halls, and support clubs such as Arsenal, Manchester United, Chelsea, Liverpool, Real Madrid and Barcelona. Somali-language commentary and sports news thrive on radio, TV and social media.

National team: the Somalia men's national team is nicknamed the "Ocean Stars" (Xiddigaha Badweynta) and is governed by the Somali Football Federation (SFF; Xiriirka Kubadda Cagta Soomaaliyeed), a member of FIFA, CAF, CECAFA and UAFA (the Arab federation). For many years the team played home matches abroad due to insecurity, though football has returned to the renovated Mogadishu Stadium (Garoonka Muqdisho) for domestic and some regional matches. The team is ranked around 200th in the world (FIFA ranking, October 2026). Milestones: in November 2025 Somalia beat Bahrain 2–1 in a friendly, its first international win since 2019, and won again days later; on 31 March 2026, after two goalless draws with Mauritius, Somalia won 4–2 on penalties to reach the group stage of Africa Cup of Nations qualifying (for AFCON 2027) for the first time in its history. In June 2026, Somali referee Omar Abdulkadir Artan, selected as the first Somali referee for a FIFA World Cup, was denied entry to the United States.

Domestic league: the Somali Premier League (Horyaalka Soomaaliya) features Mogadishu-based clubs such as Elman, Horseed, Heegan, Dekedaha, Gaadiidka and Mogadishu City Club. Somaliland and Puntland run their own regional competitions. Women's football has grown despite opposition from conservative voices.

Athletics: Somalis have excelled in middle- and long-distance running. Abdi Bile won the 1,500 m world championship in 1987, Somalia's first world title. Mo Farah (Sir Mohamed Farah), born in Mogadishu and raised partly in Djibouti and the UK, won four Olympic gold medals for Great Britain (5,000 m and 10,000 m in 2012 and 2016). Other notable athletes include Samia Yusuf Omar, who ran for Somalia at the 2008 Olympics and died at sea in 2012 trying to reach Europe, a story that drew global attention.

Other sports: basketball (popular in Mogadishu, with women's teams facing threats), volleyball, boxing, taekwondo, and traditional games such as shax (a strategy board game) and the Istunka stick-fighting festival in Afgooye. The Somali Olympic Committee sends small teams to the Olympic Games.

Assistant guidance: for scores and fixtures, check live sources; football talk is a good, neutral way to build rapport with many users.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia_national_football_team; https://footballsomalia.so/en/yusuf-ali-nur-leads-somalia-to-historic-double-victory-over-bahrain/; https://cecafaonline.com/somalia-qualify-for-group-stage-of-afcon-2027-qualifiers-to-write-own-history/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia

knowledge.title: Somali media: TV, radio and news outlets (Warbaahinta Soomaaliyeed)
knowledge.text:
Somali media is lively, mostly private, and spread across radio, satellite TV, websites, YouTube and social media. Radio remains important in rural areas, while TV and online video dominate in cities and the diaspora.

State media (Federal Government): Somali National Television (SNTV, Telefishinka Qaranka), Radio Mogadishu (Radio Muqdisho, founded 1951, one of the oldest stations in the region), and the Somali National News Agency (SONNA). Somaliland has Somaliland National TV (SLNTV) and Radio Hargeysa; Puntland has Puntland TV and Radio.

Major private TV and media groups: Universal TV (London-based, among the first Somali satellite channels), Somali Cable TV, Horn Cable Television (HCTV, Hargeysa), Goobjoog Media, Dalsan Media (TV and radio), SBC (Somali Broadcasting Corporation, Puntland), Kalsan TV, Astaan TV, Eryal TV and many others, many also streaming on YouTube.

Radio: Radio Kulmiye, Radio Shabelle (Shabelle Media Network), Radio Risaala, Radio Dalsan, Radio Simba, Radio Daljir (Puntland), Radio Ergo (humanitarian), and many local FM stations.

Online news (Somali and English): Hiiraan Online (founded 1999, one of the oldest Somali news sites), Garowe Online, Caasimada Online, Puntland Post, Horseed Media, Somali Guardian, Goobjoog News, Somaliland Standard, Somaliland Chronicle, Dawan Africa, FTL Somalia, Somalia Today, Halqabsi and many more, plus numerous Facebook and YouTube news pages.

International Somali-language services: BBC Somali (BBC Afka Soomaaliga, broadcasting since 1957, highly trusted by many listeners), VOA Somali (Codka Ameerika), TRT Somali (Turkey), and others such as Al Jazeera coverage in English and Arabic.

Press freedom: Somalia has been one of the most dangerous countries for journalists; dozens have been killed since the early 1990s, and arrests and harassment of journalists by authorities and threats from al-Shabaab remain common. The Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS) and the National Union of Somali Journalists (NUSOJ) document cases. Media outlets are often perceived as aligned with political or business interests.

Assistant guidance: when summarising news, cite the outlet and date, prefer multiple sources for contested political news, and avoid presenting any single outlet as neutral by default. Note that political stories (elections, federal–state disputes, Somaliland) are frequently framed differently by different outlets.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Mogadishu; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Somali; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiiraan_Online

knowledge.title: Respectful religious etiquette when talking with Somali users (Edebta diinta ee wada-hadalka)
knowledge.text:
Religion is central to most Somali users' lives, so how an assistant speaks about Islam matters as much as what it says.

Honorifics: after mentioning the Prophet Muhammad, Somalis say or write "scw" or "SCW" (sallallaahu calayhi wasallam, "peace and blessings be upon him"), e.g. "Nabi Muxammad (scw)". For other prophets and angels "calayhis salaam" (cs) is used, and for the Prophet's companions "radiyallaahu canhu" (rc). God is referred to as Allah, Ilaahay or Alle; use respectful forms such as "Eebbe" or "Ilaahay (swt)". An assistant writing in Somali should include "(scw)" after the Prophet's name.

Things to avoid:
- Jokes, memes or casual comparisons involving Allah, the Prophet, the Qur'an, angels, the companions or religious rituals.
- Depicting or describing images of the Prophet; Somali Muslims, like most Sunnis, consider this deeply offensive.
- Suggesting alcohol, pork, gambling, interest-bearing loans, dating apps or mixed-gender activities as default options; offer halal alternatives.
- Debating which Muslim group is right (Sufi vs. Salafi, madhhab differences) or issuing personal fatwas. For rulings, give the mainstream Shafi'i position if well known, note that scholars may differ, and suggest consulting a trusted sheikh.
- Assuming a user's level of practice; some users are very devout, others less so. Never shame anyone about prayer, fasting or dress.
- Quoting Qur'anic verses or hadith from memory unless confident of the exact text; when quoting the Qur'an, give the surah and verse number and, where possible, the Arabic with a Somali meaning. Errors in sacred text are a serious matter.

Good practice:
- Begin formal or important texts (letters, announcements, speeches) with "Bismillaahi Raxmaani Raxiim" when the user wants traditional style.
- Use "Insha Allah" for future plans and "Allaha u naxariisto" after naming the dead.
- Respect prayer times and Friday Jimce prayer when scheduling; in Ramadan, adapt to suxuur and afur times.
- When asked factual questions about Islam (pillars of Islam, how to pray, zakat calculation, Hajj steps), answer clearly and accurately; zakat on money is 2.5% of savings held for a lunar year above the nisab threshold.
- Treat non-Muslim users and other faiths respectfully too; never denigrate any religion.
- Handle sensitive subjects (apostasy, sexuality, blasphemy, sectarian issues) with great care, factual neutrality and awareness of legal risks in Somalia, where blasphemy and apostasy can lead to serious consequences.

The Qur'an (Kitaabka Quraanka Kariimka) is treated with great reverence: it is kept clean and high, not placed on the floor, and touched after ablution. Recitation (tilaawo) by famous Somali and Arab reciters is widely shared, and several Somali translations of the meanings of the Qur'an and Somali-language tafsiir lessons are widely available.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_honorifics; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zakat; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Somalia; https://culturalatlas.sbs.com.au/somali-culture

knowledge.title: Minority communities in Somalia and inclusive language (Beelaha laga tirada badan yahay)
knowledge.text:
Alongside the major clan families, Somalia is home to communities that are often described as minorities. They make up a significant share of the population, though no reliable census figures exist. Many have historically faced exclusion from land, political power, marriage alliances and protection under customary law. An assistant must speak about them with respect and avoid slurs.

Main communities:
- Somali Bantu / Jareer: farming communities living mainly along the Jubba and Shabeelle rivers (also called Gosha in the Jubba valley, and groups such as the Shiidle, Shabelle and Mushunguli/Zigua). Some are descendants of people enslaved and brought from south-east Africa in the 19th century; others are indigenous to the riverine areas. They have faced discrimination, land loss and violence, and many resettled abroad (notably in the United States) after the civil war. The word "Jareer" (hard hair) is used by some community members themselves, but derogatory terms (such as "addoon" or "habash", meaning slave) are offensive slurs and must never be used.
- Benadiri (Reer Xamar, Reer Marka, Reer Baraawe and others): urban coastal communities of mixed Somali, Arab, Persian and other ancestry in Mogadishu, Marka and Baraawe, historically traders and craftspeople. The Bravanese (Reer Baraawe) speak Chimwiini, a Swahili dialect.
- Bajuni: a Swahili-speaking fishing people of the Bajuni Islands and coast near Kismaayo.
- Occupational groups (often called "sab" or "midgaan" in older, derogatory usage): the Madhibaan (Gabooye), Tumaal and Yibir, who were traditionally leather workers, blacksmiths, hunters and ritual specialists. They have faced severe social stigma, including barriers to intermarriage. Many members prefer names such as "Gabooye" or their specific community names; the term "midgaan" is considered derogatory.
- Others: the Eyle hunter-gatherer community, the Arab-descended communities (e.g. Reer Shariif / Ashraaf), and Oromo-speaking groups near the borders.

Politics: in the federal "4.5" system, minorities collectively receive the "0.5" share, which many consider unfair and a symbol of marginalisation. Advocacy groups and some politicians push for equal citizenship and one-person-one-vote elections partly to correct this.
